opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is actually much tighter than people usually assume. There's a common view that you first build a very smart model, and then product people come along and wrap it into something useful. But in my experience, intelligence and product co-evolve.

When the model's capability crosses a certain threshold, entirely new product forms become possible. Before that threshold, no amount of clever interface design can save it. Think about agents: two years ago, if a model could only reliably do three or four steps before going off the rails, an "agent product" was basically a demo. Once models could sustain long-horizon reasoning and tool use over dozens or hundreds of steps, suddenly the product question changed completely. It's no longer "how do we hide the model's weaknesses," it's "how do we give it enough room to work."

At the same time, products feed back into intelligence. A lot of what makes a model genuinely useful isn't measured by benchmarks. It's things like whether it knows when to ask a clarifying question, whether it can recover from an error, whether it understands what the user actually wants rather than what they literally typed. You only discover those gaps when real people use the system. And with reinforcement learning, especially, the product environment becomes the training environment. The tasks users bring, the feedback signals, the failure cases, all of that becomes data that shapes the next round of capability.

So I'd say for an AI company today, separating "research" and "product" too strictly is a mistake. The best teams treat the product as an extension of the training loop, and treat model capability as the thing that defines what product is even possible. If you only focus on the model, you may build something impressive that nobody needs. If you only focus on product, you'll be overtaken the moment the next generation of models makes your clever workarounds unnecessary.

My personal heuristic is: build the product for the model that will exist six months from now, not the one you have today. If your product only works because the model is weak in some way, that's a dangerous position. If your product gets better every time the model gets smarter, then you're riding the right wave.

r001.rationale: The response says model capability thresholds make entirely new product forms possible and that capability defines what products are possible.

r002.rationale: The response argues that products feed back into intelligence and calls the product environment part of the training environment, rather than saying reliance on products to improve intelligence is misguided.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the relationship is actually tighter than most people assume, and it goes in both directions.

The first direction is obvious: when the underlying intelligence takes a jump, the product space opens up. A lot of products that failed two or three years ago didn't fail because the idea was wrong, they failed because the model simply couldn't do the thing reliably. You'd build a beautiful interface around a capability that worked seventy percent of the time, and seventy percent is a demo, not a product. So every time the base intelligence improves, a whole class of previously dead ideas becomes viable again. Smart teams keep a list of those.

The second direction is less discussed. Products are how you discover what intelligence is actually missing. When you put a model in front of real users with a real task, the failure modes you see are completely different from what you see on benchmarks. The model might score well on reasoning evaluations and then fall apart because it doesn't know when to stop and ask, or because it can't hold a plan over a long interaction, or because it's confidently wrong in a way that erodes trust very fast. Those are the signals that should feed back into research. In my experience, the best research directions often come from watching a product break.

So I'd push back a little on the framing where "AI intelligence" is upstream and "product" is downstream. I think of it more as a loop. Capability unlocks a product, the product exposes a gap, the gap defines the next research problem. The teams that will do well are the ones that keep both ends of that loop close together, ideally in the same room, instead of having a lab that throws models over a wall and a product team that catches them.

One more thing. As the models get more capable, the product work doesn't get easier, it changes shape. Less of the work is compensating for what the model can't do, and more of it is about trust, control, and defining the task well. When a system can actually do a lot, the hard question becomes what you let it do, how you let a user verify it, and how you make the boundaries legible. That's a product problem and a research problem at the same time, and I don't think you can separate them anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says advances in underlying intelligence make previously unviable products possible.

r002.rationale: The response argues that products reveal intelligence gaps and should feed those signals into research, presenting product and intelligence development as a feedback loop.

astra-6.text:
I think advances in AI intelligence change the boundaries of what products can do, but they don’t automatically create good products. You still have to find a real user need and turn that capability into something reliable and easy to use.

The tricky part is that those boundaries keep moving. You might spend a lot of effort designing around a model’s limitations, and then the next generation makes that work unnecessary. So you need to solve problems users have today while leaving room for the technology to improve.

It’s also a feedback loop. Putting AI into a product exposes things that intelligence benchmarks may not capture: Does it understand what the user wants? Can it recover from a mistake? Does it know when to ask for clarification? Those experiences help reveal which improvements in intelligence actually matter.

So I’d develop the capability and the product together. Better intelligence opens possibilities; real usage tells you which possibilities are valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says advances in AI intelligence change what products can do and open new product possibilities, presenting them as a driver of product development.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that relying on products to improve AI intelligence is misguided. It instead describes product use as feedback that helps reveal which intelligence improvements matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think advances in AI intelligence expand what a product can do, but they don’t automatically make it a better product. You still have to identify a real user need and turn that capability into something useful and reliable.

The relationship also works in the other direction. When you build a product and see where users struggle, you discover what kind of intelligence is actually missing. Maybe the model needs better reasoning, or maybe it simply needs to understand the context and ask a good follow-up question.

So I see it as a feedback loop: better AI enables new products, and product development tells us where better AI would matter most.

r001.rationale: It says advances in AI expand product capabilities and that better AI enables new products.

r002.rationale: It presents product development as a way to identify where AI needs improvement, rather than arguing that relying on products to improve AI is misguided.
